parametric-motion-s1.title: Graphs of $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ for a moving particle
parametric-motion-s1.text: A particle moves in the plane with position $(x(t), y(t))$ for $0 \le t \le 4$, where $x(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t$ and $y(t) = 4t - t^2$. The graph shows each coordinate against time.

plot.label: Graphs of x(t) = t cubed minus 6t squared plus 9t and y(t) = 4t minus t squared against t for t from 0 to 4

parametric-motion-s2.title: A thrown ball
parametric-motion-s2.text: A ball is thrown from a height of 1.5 meters. Seen from the side, its position $t$ seconds after the throw is $(x(t), y(t))$, in meters.

table.caption: The model for the ball: horizontal distance x(t) and height y(t), in meters, t seconds after the throw

items.q: On which interval is the particle moving to the left?

why.correct: The particle moves left where $x(t)$ is decreasing. The graph of $x(t)$ falls from $4$ at $t = 1$ to $0$ at $t = 3$.
options: $x(t)$ decreases on $(1, 3)$: left.
$x(t)$ increases on $(0, 1)$, so the particle moves right.
$y(t)$ decreases on $(2, 4)$; that is when the particle moves down.
$y(t)$ increases on $(0, 2)$; that is when it moves up.

items.q: Where is the particle when it is highest?

why.correct: The particle is highest where $y(t)$ is largest: $y(2) = 4$. Its position then is $(x(2), y(2)) = (8 - 24 + 18, 4) = (2, 4)$.
options: The coordinates are swapped; $x$ comes first.
$(4, 3)$ is the point at $t = 1$, where the particle is farthest right, not highest.
$(0, 3)$ is the point at $t = 3$, after the particle has started down.

items.q: On which interval is the particle moving left and down at the same time?

why.correct: Left needs $x(t)$ decreasing, on $(1, 3)$. Down needs $y(t)$ decreasing, on $(2, 4)$. Both hold on the overlap, $(2, 3)$.
options: The overlap of $(1, 3)$ and $(2, 4)$ is $(2, 3)$.
On $(1, 2)$, $y(t)$ is still increasing, so the particle moves left and up.
On $(3, 4)$, $x(t)$ increases again: right and down.
This is the whole time it moves left, but for $1 < t < 2$ it is moving up.

items.q: At which times in $[0, 4]$ is the particle farthest to the right? Select all that apply.

why.correct: Farthest right means the largest $x(t)$. The graph of $x(t)$ reaches $4$ twice, at $t = 1$ and at $t = 4$, and is below $4$ everywhere else.
options: $x(1) = 4$, the largest value.
$x(2) = 2$; $t = 2$ is when the particle is highest.
$x(3) = 0$; this is when it is farthest left.
$x(4) = 4$, tied for the largest value.

items.q: At $t = 1$, $x(t)$ changes from increasing to decreasing. Is the particle at rest at $t = 1$?
options: No: $y(t)$ is still increasing then, so the particle is moving up
Yes: $x(t)$ stops changing, so the particle stops
Yes: the particle is at its highest point then
No: $x(t)$ is still increasing at $t = 1$

why.correct: Only the horizontal motion turns around at $t = 1$. $y(t) = 4t - t^2$ increases until $t = 2$, so at $t = 1$ the particle is still rising. It is not at rest.
options: The vertical motion continues: $y(t)$ increases on $(0, 2)$.
A stop needs both coordinates to stop changing; $y(t)$ keeps increasing.
The highest point is at $t = 2$, where $y(2) = 4$.
$x(t)$ reaches its largest value at $t = 1$; it is turning around, not still increasing.

items.q: At what time does the ball hit the ground? Give your answer correct to three decimal places.

mistakes.why: That zero is before the throw. Keep the zero with $t > 0$.
That solves $-4.9t^2 + 12t = 0$ and drops the starting height of 1.5 meters.

why.correct: The ball is on the ground when $y(t) = 0$. Graph $-4.9x^2 + 12x + 1.5$ and find its zeros: $-0.119$ and $2.568$. Only $t > 0$ makes sense, so $t \approx 2.568$ seconds.

items.q: How far from the thrower, horizontally, does the ball land? Give your answer correct to three decimal places.

mistakes.why: This uses the landing time without the 1.5 meter start. Solve $-4.9t^2 + 12t + 1.5 = 0$.
Rounding the time to $2.57$ before multiplying changes the third decimal. Store the time and use the stored value.

why.correct: Store the landing time from $-4.9t^2 + 12t + 1.5 = 0$, $t \approx 2.568178$. Then $x \approx 15(2.568178) \approx 38.523$ meters.

items.q: What is the greatest height the ball reaches? Give your answer in meters, correct to three decimal places.

mistakes.why: That is the time of the top, $t = \frac{12}{9.8}$; put it into $y(t)$.
This leaves out the starting height; $y(t)$ includes the $+ 1.5$.

why.correct: $y(t)$ is a parabola opening down. Its vertex is at $t = \frac{-12}{2(-4.9)} \approx 1.2245$ (or use the calculator's maximum). Store it: $y \approx 8.847$ meters.

items.q: At what times is the ball 6 meters high?
options: $t \approx 0.462$ and $t \approx 1.987$
$t \approx 0.462$, the one time on the way up
$t \approx 1.987$, the one time on the way down
$t \approx 1.224$, when the ball is at the top

why.correct: Solve $-4.9t^2 + 12t + 1.5 = 6$: graph $y = -4.9x^2 + 12x + 1.5$ and $y = 6$ and find every intersection. They are at $t \approx 0.462$ (going up) and $t \approx 1.987$ (coming down).
options: The ball passes 6 meters twice, once rising and once falling.
The ball also passes 6 meters on the way down; find every intersection.
The ball also passes 6 meters on the way up, near $t = 0.462$.
At the top the ball is about $8.847$ meters high, above 6 meters.

items.q: For which times does the model describe the ball?
options: $t \ge 0$

why.correct: The model starts at the throw, $t = 0$, and ends when the ball lands, $t \approx 2.568$. After that $y(t)$ is negative, a height a ball resting on the ground cannot have.
options: From the throw until the landing.
After $t \approx 2.568$ the model gives negative heights.
This stops at the top of the flight; the ball keeps moving until it lands.
Times before the throw, $t < 0$, are not part of the flight.

items.q: How does the graph of $x(t)$ against $t$ differ from the path of the particle?
options: The graph of $x(t)$ shows when the particle moves right or left; the path shows where it goes
They are the same picture drawn with different labels on the axes
The graph of $x(t)$ shows the path, and the path shows the time
The graph of $x(t)$ shows where the particle is highest

why.correct: The graph of $x(t)$ puts time across and horizontal position up, so its rises and falls show right and left motion. The path plots $y$ against $x$ and leaves time out.
options: Against $t$: direction in $x$. In the plane: the path.
The axes differ ($t$ and $x$ versus $x$ and $y$), so the shapes usually differ too.
The path is $y$ against $x$; time is not on either of its axes.
Height is $y(t)$; the graph of $x(t)$ says nothing about it.

items.q: A particle moves with $x(t) = 2t - 3$ and $y(t) = t^2 - 4t$ for $0 \le t \le 5$. What is its $x$-coordinate when it is at its lowest point?

mistakes.why: $t = 2$ is the time of the lowest point. Its $x$-coordinate is $x(2) = 2(2) - 3$.
$-4$ is the lowest $y$-value, $y(2)$. The question asks for $x(2)$.

why.correct: $y(t) = t^2 - 4t = (t - 2)^2 - 4$ is lowest at $t = 2$. Then $x(2) = 2(2) - 3 = 1$, so the lowest point is $(1, -4)$.

items.q: A robot starts at $x = 5$ meters and moves left at a constant 2 meters per second. Write its horizontal position $x(t)$ after $t$ seconds.

mistakes.why: Moving left makes $x$ smaller, so subtract: $5 - 2t$.
At $t = 0$ the robot is at $x = 5$, so the constant term is $+5$.
The robot starts at $x = 5$, not at $0$: add the starting position.

why.correct: Start at $5$ and lose $2$ meters each second: $x(t) = 5 - 2t$.

items.q: A particle follows $(x(t), y(t))$ for $0 \le t \le 6$. A second particle follows $(x(2t), y(2t))$ for $0 \le t \le 3$. Predict how the second compares with the first.

variables.name: The set of points it passes through
variables.why: As $t$ runs over $[0, 3]$, $2t$ runs over $[0, 6]$, so it visits exactly the same points.

variables.name: The time it takes to cover the whole path
variables.why: It finishes at $t = 3$ instead of $t = 6$: the same trip in half the time.

why.correct: Doubling the input speeds up the trip without changing the path or where it starts.

items.q: On $0 < t < 3$, $x(t)$ is increasing and $y(t)$ is decreasing. Which statements are true on that interval? Select all that apply.
options: The particle moves right
The particle moves down
The particle moves up
The path is a straight line

why.correct: $x(t)$ increasing means moving right; $y(t)$ decreasing means moving down. The shape of the path is not given.
options: $x(t)$ increases: right.
$y(t)$ decreases: down.
Up would need $y(t)$ increasing.
Right and down can follow a curve; directions alone do not make a straight line.

items.q: Put the steps for describing a particle's motion from $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ in order.
options: Find where $x(t)$ increases and where it decreases
Find where $y(t)$ increases and where it decreases
Split the time interval at each turning point of $x(t)$ or $y(t)$
On each piece, combine right or left with up or down

why.correct: Read each coordinate separately, cut time at every turnaround, then describe each piece with one horizontal and one vertical direction.
